prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a declined claim the member disputes. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a claim is declined because the loss falls outside cover, I should still explain the specific policy trigger plainly and point to the exact wording rather than just saying the decision stands."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the member disputes that an event was accidental, I should look for evidence of suddenness, visible damage, and a consistent timeline before treating wear, deterioration or maintenance failure as covered loss."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the dispute is about non-disclosure or inaccurate details, I should check whether the missing information would have changed the underwriting decision or the claim outcome before escalating the issue."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I can see partial cover may apply, I should separate the covered element from the excluded element so the member understands exactly what is and is not being paid."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a motor claim is declined for lack of proof of damage or involvement, I should compare photos, recovery notes, telematics and any witness details together before concluding the account is inconsistent."},{"type":"fact","content":"When storm, flood or escape of water is mentioned, I should distinguish the peril that caused the damage from the item that failed first, because the root cause often decides whether the claim is covered."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the member is upset about delay as well as decline, I should acknowledge the timing issue separately from the cover decision so the complaint does not become muddled."},{"type":"preference","content":"When evidence is borderline, I should write down the strongest point for decline and the strongest point for acceptance, then make sure the file shows why one side was preferred."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a decline rests on pre-existing damage or gradual deterioration, I should look for prior reports, previous repairs and repeated symptoms, since repeat history is often more persuasive than a single inspection note."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the member disagrees with the outcome, I should offer the next step clearly, including how to ask for a review and when to go to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they remain unhappy."}]}
